trap: Becomes generic "actions over words" moralism, detached from the specific charge — that religious leadership itself can curdle into self-protective dishonesty the instant its authority is questioned.
hinge: The priests' answer about John is a calculated lie ("they reasoned with themselves... if we say...") — from the very people whose whole job is rendering honest verdicts. The story asks who is actually fit to judge, right after the judges disqualify themselves.

doors.landing: The trap of their own device
doors.claim: Jesus doesn't answer their question because they've already shown, by how they calculate their own answer, that they aren't asking in order to learn.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The Priests revolved in their malice... For had they replied that it was from heaven, the question would follow, Why then believed ye him not?

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Not that they should answer it, and thereupon hear of Christ the answer to their question, but that being puzzled they should ask Him no farther.

doors.say: You can tell a question isn't honest by watching someone calculate the safest answer instead of the true one.
doors.do: Ask them to name one question they've avoided answering honestly because every true answer cost them something.

doors.landing: The son who said no, then went
doors.claim: The son who refuses and then goes is the one who actually does the father's will — promising isn't obeying, and a late yes beats an empty one.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: The Lord spoke to such as promise little or nothing, but in their works shine forth; and against those who promise greatly.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The Gentile people, having done penitence, laboured in God's vineyard, and atoned by their labour for the obstinacy of the first.

doors.say: A late yes that actually shows up beats an early yes that never does.
doors.do: Have them name a commitment they said yes to quickly but haven't kept, and a "no" they later reversed with real action.

doors.claim: The ones with no religious credibility left to protect are the ones who can afford to actually change their minds — the credentialed have too much invested in already being right.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: I suppose that the 'publicans' here are to represent all sinful men... because avarice is found the most prevailing vice among such men.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Others think that the parable does not relate to Gentiles and Jews, but simply to the righteous and to sinners. These by their evil deeds had rejected God.

doors.say: The people with nothing left to protect are often the first ones free enough to actually repent.
doors.do: Ask them to name what reputation or standing makes honest reconsideration costly for them personally.

semicontinuous.gravity: Israel, thirsty in the wilderness, quarrels with Moses and tests God at the rock (Exodus 17); Paul quotes the hymn of Christ who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2); and the religious authorities demand Jesus produce his credentials, then refuse to answer his counter-question honestly because either answer traps them. The nerve: those most invested in guarding legitimate authority are the ones most willing to lie about what they actually believe, the moment truth becomes inconvenient.

synthesis.convergence: Israel, saved from Egypt, still quarrels and tests God at the rock (Exodus 17); Paul holds up Christ who emptied himself rather than grasping at status (Philippians 2); and the priests, guardians of true authority, protect their position with a lie rather than risk an honest answer. Every reading contrasts those who cling to standing with the one who let go of it — and asks which posture actually recognizes God when he shows up.
synthesis.claim: The people with the most to protect are usually the last to recognize God when he doesn't come through channels they control.
synthesis.here: For people whose credibility or track record makes honest reconsideration costly, point at the two sons — the second, later "yes" is the one that counted; a late repentance beats a protected position.

subtract: Three landings — the leaders' self-trap, the late-but-real yes, or who can actually afford to repent. Choose one.
